topic.title: Turtle Library Overview
topic.description: Explores Turtle module attributes: printing the turtle object reference and reading screen canvas dimensions. Builds familiarity with the turtle environment.

learningNotes.whatILearned: Turtle is a library: you import the classes you want and the objects they make are yours to drive.
learningNotes.challenges: The comments name what each line does instead of saying why any of it is there.
learningNotes.nextSteps: Rewrite the three comments so they say what the file is showing rather than what the code is calling.

files.description: Prints turtle object info and screen canvas width.

misconceptions: `print(timmi)` shows the object reference, not the turtle — that is the point of the line, and the comment should say so
`import turtle as t` and `from turtle import Turtle` are different styles, and the file shows both
engine.review:
**The rubric I used**

There is no task sheet for this one — it was written before the engine
existed, so there was nothing to grade it against. I graded the file on the
three things that have always mattered here:

- **40 — it runs.** It compiles or interprets without an error.
- **30 — it is right.** The output is what it claims to produce.
- **30 — it explains itself.** Comments say *why*, not *what*.

**0 + 30 + 10 = 40%**

**This file cannot be run here.** It needs `tkinter`, and this
machine has no display and no `tkinter` — so the 40 points for *it runs* are
not ones I can give, and they are not given. The other two bands are judged
by reading the code, carefully, line by line.

There is a bigger point here, and it is worth saying plainly: **`tkinter`
does not exist on Termux either.** These files cannot be run on the phone
this whole system is built around. They are not broken — they are stranded.

**What is right, by reading**

It is the clearest of the turtle files, and it has the three comments the others lack. `print(timmi)` deliberately prints the object reference to show what a turtle *is* in Python — a bound method, not a picture of a turtle — and the comment says exactly that. `canvwidth` shows the canvas is 300 wide by default, and the last line keeps the window open so you can look at it.

**What is not**

The comments say what the code does rather than why it is there: *Shows turtle object reference* describes the `print`, it does not explain that seeing the reference is the lesson. And *Corrected variable name* is a note to yourself, not an explanation to a reader.

**The one thing to fix first**

```python
print(timmi)  # A turtle in Python is a bound method, not a picture - this shows it.
```

That one line turns the file from a list of calls into an explanation of what a turtle actually is.
